# ![[Uncaptioned image]](2610.25078v1/coevorsi-title.png) When Harnesses Evolve, Which Models Should Follow?

Jiaqi Su Affiliation: Tiankuo Yao, Ivor Tsang, Haiyan Yin, Shuicheng YAN
   Guibin Zhang Affiliation: National University of Singapore   
Jie-Jing Shao Affiliation: Agency for Science, Technology and Research
(A\*STAR)    Cong Pang Affiliation: SenseTime Group Inc.

###### Abstract

Model–harness co-evolution has emerged as a prominent paradigm for
recursive self-improving (RSI) agents, jointly evolving their execution
scaffolds and intrinsic capabilities. We study the persistent yet often
overlooked _brain–body mismatch problem_ in this paradigm, where an
evolving harness (body) demands behaviors its model (brain) has not
learned or restricts capabilities it already possesses. We introduce
CoEvo-RSI, a RSI framework that advances model–harness co-evolution
through agent-driven, bidirectional historical inheritance. Drawing on a
shared evolutionary archive and execution feedback, a meta-agent
coordinates harness development from historical designs with model
checkpoint selection or merging and subsequent adaptation under the
selected harness, aligning inherited capabilities with evolving
execution requirements to reduce brain–body mismatch. Using only
supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on its own rejection-sampled trajectories,
CoEvo-RSI makes Qwen3.5-9B competitive with larger models across diverse
vertical applications, including multi-agent failure attribution,
role-aware text-to-SQL, and smart-home instruction following. It
surpasses DeepSeek-V4-Pro on TraceElephant ($`+14.16`$ agent accuracy)
and GLM-5.3 on HomeBench VM ($`+4.90`$ success rate), underscoring the
need for brain–body alignment and the potential of bidirectional
historical inheritance to advance agent co-evolution.

## 1  Introduction

An agent’s capabilities depend jointly on its _brain_—the language model
that reasons and selects actions—and its _body_—the harness that defines
its tool interfaces, action space, memory, and execution workflow ([Lou
et al., 2026](#bib.bib26); [Chen et al., 2026c](#bib.bib9)).
Accordingly, progress has followed two complementary directions. Model
training improves the agent’s learned policy through supervised
learning, reinforcement learning, and self-distillation ([Xia et al.,
2026](#bib.bib56); [Yang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib60); [Zhang et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib70)). Harness optimization improves the surrounding
system with the model fixed, through iterative modification of prompts,
tools, and control flow guided by execution feedback ([Lou et al.,
2026](#bib.bib26); [Lin et al., 2026](#bib.bib22)), or population-based
evolution that generates, evaluates, and recombines competing harness
designs ([Lee et al., 2026c](#bib.bib20); [Zhang et al.,
2026h](#bib.bib78)). These directions meet in model–harness
co-evolution, where model training and harness optimization jointly
adapt an agent to its task domain ([Chen et al., 2026c](#bib.bib9); [Luo
et al., 2026a](#bib.bib30)). Recent systems demonstrate the promise of
this approach across tool use, mathematical reasoning, search-based
question answering, and chess ([Chen et al., 2026b](#bib.bib8); [Chen
et al., 2026d](#bib.bib10); [Kim et al., 2026](#bib.bib17)).

A co-evolution round couples harness evolution with model adaptation.
Starting from a model–harness pair $`(\mathbf{H}_{t},\theta_{t})`$,
execution feedback $`\mathbf{F}_{t}`$ guides changes to the harness,
whose requirements in turn shape the model’s next adaptation ([Chen
et al., 2026d](#bib.bib10)). As either component evolves, the harness’s
execution requirements and the model’s learned capabilities can drift
apart. In this setting, we first identify and formalize the brain–body
mismatch problem:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 2: Brain–body alignment in model–harness co-evolution. Left:
Historical harnesses and checkpoints are recombined and adapted to
resolve interface mismatch. Right: Step accuracy versus Turn-level
Interface Mismatch Rate (TIMR;
[Section 3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Model–Harness Co-Evolution ‣ 3 Method ‣ When Harnesses Evolve, Which Models Should Follow?"))
for ten evolved versions per method, from a three-round run evaluated on
the Who&When test benchmark.

In plain terms, the model may struggle to operate its harness, and the
harness may underuse its model’s abilities
([Figure 2](#S1.F2 "In 1 Introduction ‣ When Harnesses Evolve, Which Models Should Follow?")).
Consider two concrete examples. ❶ *Interface mismatch.* The model emits
XML tool calls, while the evolved harness expects JSON, causing
otherwise correct calls to be rejected. ❷ *Capability mismatch.* The
harness introduces an _active context management tool_ for deciding what
information to retain, summarize, or discard. A model unfamiliar with
these operations may use it poorly; a historical checkpoint
$`\theta_{i}`$ already possesses the relevant capabilities and provides
a suitable starting point for adaptation. On the harness side, a
historical design $`\mathbf{H}_{j}`$ can supply an execution workflow
suited to the model’s capabilities. These examples motivate selecting
predecessors whose inherited behaviors and structures support further
evolution.

To address this challenge, we propose CoEvo-RSI, a framework for
model–harness co-evolution through bidirectional historical inheritance.
Its evolutionary archive $`\mathbf{A}_{<t}`$ records earlier harnesses,
model checkpoints, their development histories, and execution outcomes.
Each round begins with feedback from the current pair. A Curator
organizes this evidence, and harness editors browse the archive, choose
their own historical starting designs, and develop offspring harnesses.
For each offspring, the framework selects or merges historical
checkpoints to form candidate model–harness pairs. Evaluation identifies
a promising pair for model adaptation under its harness, and validation
determines which pair advances to the next round. The resulting designs,
checkpoints, and outcomes extend the archive. This agent-driven
inheritance connects the two sides of evolution: harness design draws on
accumulated structural experience, while model initialization draws on
capabilities suited to the emerging harness. Their coordination makes
_brain–body alignment_ the organizing principle of the evolutionary
process. Our contributions are:

- •
  Problem Formalization. We formalize brain–body mismatch in
  model–harness co-evolution and introduce the turn-level interface
  mismatch rate (TIMR) as an inexpensive diagnostic signal for
  observable interface violations.
- •
  Method Design. We propose CoEvo-RSI, which combines an evolutionary
  archive with bidirectional historical inheritance. Harness editors
  select historical starting designs, and model inheritance selects or
  merges checkpoints to support adaptation under the evolved harness.
- •
  Empirical Evaluation. We evaluate CoEvo-RSI across multi-agent failure
  attribution, home care, and SQL tasks, with co-evolved Qwen3.5-9B
  outperforming Qwen3.8-Max on Who&When Pro ($`+4.40`$ agent acc.) and
  DeepSeek-V4-Pro on TraceElephant ($`+14.16`$ agent acc.).

## 2  Related Work

Self-evolving agents improve through changes to external execution
systems, learned model parameters, or both ([Gao et al.,
2026](#bib.bib12); [Guo et al., 2026](#bib.bib13); [Wang et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib52)). We organize the literature around these
optimization targets and the reuse of historical components that
connects them.

#### Recursive Harness Improvement.

Early agent systems established how external organization can improve a
model’s behavior: ReAct interleaves reasoning and actions, Reflexion
retains verbal feedback across trials, and Voyager accumulates reusable
executable skills ([Yao et al., 2023](#bib.bib62); [Shinn et al.,
2023](#bib.bib46); [Wang et al., 2023](#bib.bib51)). Agent–computer
interface design further shows how the operations exposed to a model
shape its effectiveness ([Yang et al., 2024](#bib.bib59)). Subsequent
work turns these hand-designed mechanisms into optimization targets,
evolving context ([Zhang et al., 2026g](#bib.bib76)), memory ([Zhang
et al., 2025a](#bib.bib68); [Zhang et al., 2026e](#bib.bib73); [Pan
et al., 2026b](#bib.bib37)), planning ([Liu et al., 2026b](#bib.bib24)),
and retrieval ([Lee et al., 2026b](#bib.bib19)). At the system level,
harness search jointly modifies prompts, tools, and control flow ([Lee
et al., 2026a](#bib.bib18); [Lee et al., 2026c](#bib.bib20); [Lin
et al., 2026](#bib.bib22); [Lou et al., 2026](#bib.bib26); [Zhang
et al., 2026d](#bib.bib72); [Zhang et al., 2026f](#bib.bib75)).
AutoHarness synthesizes executable support from environmental feedback,
while Meta-Harness gives its proposer access to earlier source code,
scores, and execution traces ([Lou et al., 2026](#bib.bib26); [Lee
et al., 2026c](#bib.bib20)). Such access preserves evidence that a
single scalar score or compressed reflection can omit. Online adaptation
extends this process to deployment streams and test-time feedback ([Liu
et al., 2026c](#bib.bib25); [Nie et al., 2026b](#bib.bib34); [Pan
et al., 2026a](#bib.bib36)); population search and reusable repositories
retain alternative designs for subsequent exploration ([Zhang et al.,
2026h](#bib.bib78); [Nie et al., 2026a](#bib.bib33); [Luo et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib31)). The Darwin Gödel Machine similarly grows an archive
of self-modifying agents, allowing earlier branches to become stepping
stones for later improvements ([Zhang et al., 2025c](#bib.bib74)).
Together, these approaches expand the search target from isolated
modules to complete execution systems. They also motivate preserving
design diversity and execution history, which CoEvo-RSI connects to a
corresponding archive of model checkpoints.

#### Recursive Model Improvement.

Model self-improvement converts generated experience into persistent
changes in the policy. Three learning loops are particularly relevant.
(i) Curricula adapt the source and difficulty of training problems to
the learner, including self-play, tool-oriented task generation, and
search-agent training without externally supplied demonstrations ([Zhao
et al., 2025](#bib.bib79); [Acikgoz et al., 2026](#bib.bib1); [Sundaram
et al., 2026](#bib.bib47); [Yang et al., 2026a](#bib.bib58); [Yang
et al., 2026b](#bib.bib60); [Yue et al., 2026](#bib.bib65)). The
resulting feedback loop changes which experiences the model encounters
as its competence develops. (ii) Supervision turns demonstrations,
privileged feedback, or the model’s own improved behavior into
self-distillation targets ([Zhao et al., 2026a](#bib.bib80); [Shenfeld
et al., 2026](#bib.bib43); [Hübotter et al., 2026](#bib.bib15); [Zhang
et al., 2026b](#bib.bib70); [Lu et al., 2026b](#bib.bib28)). On-policy
variants address the learner’s current behavior, making the distribution
of generated trajectories central to what can be learned. (iii)
Experience reuse extracts reusable skills and transfers their guidance
into model behavior ([Xia et al., 2026](#bib.bib56); [Zhang et al.,
2026c](#bib.bib71); [Lu et al., 2026c](#bib.bib29); [Wu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib55); [Yang et al., 2026c](#bib.bib61)). For example,
SkillRL jointly evolves a hierarchical skill library and the agent
policy, linking experience abstraction with subsequent reinforcement
learning ([Xia et al., 2026](#bib.bib56)). These mechanisms improve the
agent’s intrinsic capabilities, while the harness determines which
tools, observations, and execution constraints appear in its training
trajectories. This dependence motivates choosing model initialization
and adaptation in relation to the harness that will actually execute the
policy.

#### Model–Harness Co-Evolution.

Joint adaptation closes the loop between the environment presented to a
policy and the behavior learned under that environment. One line couples
(i) context and weights through prompt optimization, continual
adaptation, and the transfer of contextual guidance into parameters ([Lu
et al., 2026a](#bib.bib27); [Tiwari et al., 2026](#bib.bib49); [Tu
et al., 2026](#bib.bib50); [Zhao et al., 2026b](#bib.bib82)). A second
line couples (ii) executable harnesses and policies, extending
adaptation to the tools, memory, middleware, and control flow used
during rollout ([Chen et al., 2026b](#bib.bib8); [Chen et al.,
2026c](#bib.bib9); [Chen et al., 2026d](#bib.bib10); [Kim et al.,
2026](#bib.bib17); [Qi et al., 2026](#bib.bib38); [Qu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib39); [Hebbar et al., 2026](#bib.bib14); [Karten et al.,
2026](#bib.bib16); [Mao et al., 2026](#bib.bib32); [TaoLive AIGC LLM
Team et al., 2026](#bib.bib48); [Yu et al., 2026b](#bib.bib64)).
HarnessForge combines fault-guided harness tailoring with
harness-conditioned policy alignment ([Chen et al., 2026b](#bib.bib8)).
Co-Harness alternates validated harness patches with fine-tuning on
trajectories generated by the improved scaffold ([Chen et al.,
2026d](#bib.bib10)), while WHALE alternates rejection-sampling
fine-tuning with executable harness search ([Kim et al.,
2026](#bib.bib17)). A third line brings (iii) execution and editing into
a shared learning process, allowing policies to participate in the
evolution of their own support ([Luo et al., 2026a](#bib.bib30); [Shi
et al., 2026](#bib.bib45)). These methods establish the value of
adapting both sides and expose a common dependency: a harness update
changes the execution requirements, and a model update changes which
harnesses are effective. CoEvo-RSI makes _bidirectional historical
inheritance_ an explicit decision within this loop. Harness editors
choose historical starting designs, and model inheritance independently
selects or merges archived checkpoints for the resulting requirements.
This enables recovery of useful earlier capabilities without tying model
initialization to the latest generation or the harness’s parent branch.
[Appendix D](#A4 "Appendix D Comparison with Related Evolution Frameworks ‣ When Harnesses Evolve, Which Models Should Follow?")
compares the inheritance procedures of representative frameworks.

## 3  Method

CoEvo-RSI
([Figure 3](#S3.F3 "In 3 Method ‣ When Harnesses Evolve, Which Models Should Follow?"))
realizes model–harness co-evolution through bidirectional historical
inheritance. An autonomous meta-agent coordinates two complementary
decisions: harness editors select and develop historical designs, and
model inheritance selects or merges checkpoints for the resulting
execution requirements. Evaluation, model adaptation, and promotion turn
these inherited components into the next agent, whose outcomes enrich
the evolutionary archive.

Figure 3: Overview of CoEvo-RSI. Left: The Curator draws on archived
designs, checkpoints, and outcomes to guide evolution. Center: Harness
editors choose historical harness bases; checkpoint selection or merging
supplies the paired models. Right: Each round evaluates candidate pairs,
tracks TIMR, adapts the selected model to its harness, and promotes
improvements by validation performance. Outcomes return to the archive.

### 3.1  Model–Harness Co-Evolution

An executable agent is a pair $`p=(\mathbf{H},\theta)`$, where the
harness $`\mathbf{H}`$ specifies prompts, tools, state management, and
control flow, and $`\theta`$ denotes the task model’s parameters.
Constraints $`\mathbf{C}`$ fix the environment, verifier, and admissible
interfaces. Let $`\rho`$ be the task distribution and
$`\mathbf{P}_{\theta,\mathbf{H}}(\cdot\mid x;\mathbf{C})`$ the
distribution of execution trajectories for task $`x`$. A trajectory
$`\tau`$ contains model responses, tool interactions, and the final
output; its task score $`s(x,\tau)`$ is assigned by the fixed evaluator.
The objective is

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\mathbf{J}(\mathbf{H},\theta)=\mathbf{E}_{x\sim\rho}\mathbf{E}_{\tau\sim\mathbf{P}_{\theta,\mathbf{H}}(\cdot\mid x;\mathbf{C})}[s(x,\tau)],
``` |  | (1) |

where $`\mathbf{E}`$ denotes expectation. For a task set $`\mathbf{D}`$
and $`n_{\mathrm{eval}}`$ executions per task, let $`\tau_{x,u}`$ be the
trajectory from execution $`u`$. We estimate this objective by

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\widehat{\mathbf{J}}_{\mathbf{D}}(\mathbf{H},\theta)=\frac{1}{|\mathbf{D}|n_{\mathrm{eval}}}\sum_{x\in\mathbf{D}}\sum_{u=1}^{n_{\mathrm{eval}}}s(x,\tau_{x,u}).
``` |  | (2) |

For $`p=(\mathbf{H},\theta)`$, we also write
$`\widehat{\mathbf{J}}_{\mathbf{D}}(p)`$ for this estimate.

Each generation develops and adapts model–harness pairs through two
inheritance steps. A meta-agent with fixed parameters $`\phi`$ and role
policies $`\pi_{\phi}^{\mathrm{role}}`$ operates on the incumbent
$`p_{t}=(\mathbf{H}_{t},\theta_{t})`$ and an archive $`\mathbf{A}_{<t}`$
of earlier harnesses, checkpoints, and execution histories, including
the seed pair. First, the incumbent’s execution feedback
$`\mathbf{F}_{t}`$ guides the generation of $`\mathbf{K}`$ offspring
harnesses $`\mathbf{H}_{t,1:\mathbf{K}}`$ and shared evidence $`e_{t}`$:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
(\mathbf{H}_{t,1:\mathbf{K}},e_{t})=\operatorname{Inherit}_{\phi}^{\mathrm{h}}(p_{t},\mathbf{A}_{<t},\mathbf{F}_{t}),
``` |  | (3) |

where $`e_{t}`$ links historical designs to their models and outcomes.
Second, model inheritance pairs these offspring with selected or merged
checkpoints:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathbf{Q}_{t}^{\mathrm{sel}}=\operatorname{Inherit}_{\phi}^{\mathrm{m}}(\mathbf{H}_{t,1:\mathbf{K}},\mathbf{A}_{<t},e_{t}),
``` |  | (4) |

where $`\mathbf{Q}_{t}^{\mathrm{sel}}`$ is the candidate pair set.
Evaluation selects $`\bar{p}_{t}\in\mathbf{Q}_{t}^{\mathrm{sel}}`$,
adaptation produces $`p_{t}^{+}`$, and validation chooses $`p_{t+1}`$
from $`p_{t}`$, $`\bar{p}_{t}`$, and $`p_{t}^{+}`$. Completed outcomes
extend the archive to $`\mathbf{A}_{<t+1}`$.

#### Diagnosing interface mismatch.

We introduce the *Turn-level Interface Mismatch Rate* (TIMR) as a
diagnostic signal for interface mismatch. TIMR captures observable
interface violations; broader capability alignment calls for
complementary evaluation, as discussed in
[Appendix B](#A2 "Appendix B Scope and Interpretation of TIMR ‣ When Harnesses Evolve, Which Models Should Follow?").
We do not claim that TIMR fully characterizes brain–body mismatch; it
captures one aspect while serving as a cheap-to-verify and empirically
useful metric. For a pair’s evaluated trajectories
$`\mathbf{Z}(\mathbf{H},\theta)`$, let $`n_{\mathrm{lm}}(\tau)`$ count
model turns and $`v_{\tau,u}\in\{0,1\}`$ flag calls to unavailable
tools, interface-contract violations, or malformed outputs at turn
$`u`$. We define

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathbf{TIMR}(\mathbf{H},\theta)=\frac{\sum_{\tau\in\mathbf{Z}(\mathbf{H},\theta)}\sum_{u=1}^{n_{\mathrm{lm}}(\tau)}v_{\tau,u}}{\sum_{\tau\in\mathbf{Z}(\mathbf{H},\theta)}n_{\mathrm{lm}}(\tau)},
``` |  | (5) |

where each violating turn counts once, even if later recovered; lower
TIMR indicates fewer interface violations per model turn.

### 3.2  Harness Inheritance

We instantiate
[Equation 3](#S3.E3 "In 3.1 Model–Harness Co-Evolution ‣ 3 Method ‣ When Harnesses Evolve, Which Models Should Follow?")
through evidence curation and historical base selection, linking
offspring design to recorded model–harness compatibility.

#### Evidence curation.

To find designs that address the incumbent’s failures, we diagnose
observations $`\mathbf{O}_{t}`$ from $`p_{t}`$ on the validation set
$`\mathbf{V}`$, obtaining
$`\mathbf{F}_{t}=\operatorname{diagnose}(p_{t},\mathbf{O}_{t})`$. The
Curator uses this feedback to retrieve relevant history. At step $`q`$,
it chooses action $`u_{t,q}`$ from its inspection history
$`r_{t,q}^{\mathrm{cur}}`$:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
u_{t,q}\sim\pi_{\phi}^{\mathrm{ret}}\bigl(\cdot\mid\mathbf{H}_{t},\mathbf{F}_{t},\operatorname{index}(\mathbf{A}_{<t}),r_{t,q}^{\mathrm{cur}}\bigr),
``` |  | (6) |

where $`\operatorname{index}`$ exposes archive metadata. Each action and
its result $`\operatorname{read}(\mathbf{A}_{<t},u_{t,q})`$ extend the
history until the Curator stops or exhausts its retrieval budget. From
the completed history $`r_{t}^{\mathrm{cur}}`$, it constructs evidence
$`e_{t}`$ and $`\mathbf{K}`$ modification hypotheses
$`b_{t,1:\mathbf{K}}`$:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
(e_{t},b_{t,1:\mathbf{K}})\sim\pi_{\phi}^{\mathrm{cur}}\bigl(\cdot\mid\mathbf{H}_{t},\mathbf{F}_{t},r_{t}^{\mathrm{cur}};\mathbf{L}_{\mathrm{ctx}}\bigr),
``` |  | (7) |

where $`\mathbf{L}_{\mathrm{ctx}}`$ is the context-length budget.
Linking each design to its observed behavior gives editors evidence for
judging when to reuse it.

#### Historical base selection.

Different hypotheses can favor different starting designs. Each of
$`\mathbf{K}`$ independent editors receives $`b_{t,k}`$ and browses
$`\mathbf{A}_{<t}`$ to choose its own base. Its history
$`r_{t,k}^{\mathrm{edit}}`$ combines $`e_{t}`$ and $`b_{t,k}`$ with its
inspection results. With $`\mathbf{I}_{<t}`$ indexing archived
harnesses, editor $`k`$ selects

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
i_{t,k}\sim\pi_{\phi}^{\mathrm{base}}\bigl(\cdot\mid\mathbf{I}_{<t},r_{t,k}^{\mathrm{edit}}\bigr),\;\widetilde{\mathbf{H}}_{t,k}=\mathbf{H}_{i_{t,k}},
``` |  | (8) |

where $`i_{t,k}\in\mathbf{I}_{<t}`$ identifies the starting harness
$`\widetilde{\mathbf{H}}_{t,k}`$. The editor incorporates relevant
historical designs to produce

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
(\mathbf{H}_{t,k},\mathbf{U}_{t,k})\sim\pi_{\phi}^{\mathrm{edit}}\bigl(\cdot\mid\widetilde{\mathbf{H}}_{t,k},r_{t,k}^{\mathrm{edit}},\mathbf{C}\bigr),
``` |  | (9) |

where $`\mathbf{U}_{t,k}\subseteq\mathbf{I}_{<t}`$ records the harnesses
whose designs were adopted. Editors share a fixed archive; valid,
distinct offspring proceed to evaluation. Each change can thus build on
a suitable prior structure, with $`(i_{t,k},\mathbf{U}_{t,k})`$
preserving its ancestry.

### 3.3  Model Inheritance

We construct $`\mathbf{Q}_{t}^{\mathrm{sel}}`$ in
[Equation 4](#S3.E4 "In 3.1 Model–Harness Co-Evolution ‣ 3 Method ‣ When Harnesses Evolve, Which Models Should Follow?")
through checkpoint selection and merging, guided by task performance and
TIMR.

#### Model inheritance and selection.

An offspring harness changes the behaviors its model must execute,
making initialization a compatibility decision. Let $`\mathbf{M}_{<t}`$
index archived checkpoints with parameters $`\theta_{j}`$ and let
$`\boldsymbol{\alpha}=(\alpha_{j})_{j\in\mathbf{M}_{<t}}`$ denote their
weights, with $`\alpha_{j}\geq 0`$ and $`\sum_{j}\alpha_{j}=1`$. The
meta-agent directly specifies these real-valued coefficients and decides
how many merge candidates to evaluate in each round using historical
evidence and evaluation feedback. A one-hot $`\boldsymbol{\alpha}`$
selects one checkpoint; multi-checkpoint candidates use
TIES-Merging ([Yadav et al., 2023](#bib.bib57)):

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\theta(\boldsymbol{\alpha})=\operatorname{TIES}\bigl(\{\theta_{j}\}_{j\in\mathbf{M}_{<t}};\boldsymbol{\alpha}\bigr),
``` |  | (10) |

where TIES trims small task-vector entries, resolves sign conflicts, and
merges sign-consistent updates using the configuration chosen by the
meta-agent. At decision $`q`$, historical evidence $`e_{t}`$ and
evaluation feedback guide the proposal

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{t,k}^{(q)}\sim\pi_{\phi}^{\mathrm{inherit}}\bigl(\cdot\mid\mathbf{H}_{t,k},e_{t},\mathbf{M}_{<t},\mathbf{O}_{t,k}^{(q)}\bigr),
``` |  | (11) |

where $`\mathbf{O}_{t,k}^{(q)}`$ records task performance and TIMR under
$`\mathbf{H}_{t,k}`$, with both components fixed during evaluation. The
agent reads checkpoint provenance from the archive and interprets past
results in their original harness context. Preliminary evaluations
refine proposals for shortlisted harnesses, producing
$`\mathbf{Q}_{t}^{\mathrm{sel}}`$. The validation set $`\mathbf{V}`$
then determines

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\bar{p}_{t}=\underset{p\in\mathbf{Q}_{t}^{\mathrm{sel}}}{\operatorname{argmax}}\;\widehat{\mathbf{J}}_{\mathbf{V}}(p).
``` |  | (12) |

This favors initializations that can already operate the offspring
harness before adaptation.

#### Pair-specific adaptation and promotion.

To reinforce successful behavior under the selected harness,
$`\bar{p}_{t}=(\bar{\mathbf{H}}_{t},\bar{\theta}_{t})`$ generates its
own trajectories on the training set $`\mathbf{D}_{\mathrm{tr}}`$.
Rejection sampling retains its verifier-accepted executions for
supervised fine-tuning of $`\bar{\theta}_{t}`$ with
$`\bar{\mathbf{H}}_{t}`$ fixed, yielding
$`p_{t}^{+}=(\bar{\mathbf{H}}_{t},\theta_{t}^{+})`$. Promotion compares
all three stages:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
p_{t+1}=\max_{\succ_{\mathrm{prom}}}\{p_{t},\bar{p}_{t},p_{t}^{+}\},
``` |  | (13) |

where $`\succ_{\mathrm{prom}}`$ ranks eligible offspring above $`p_{t}`$
by score on the same validation set $`\mathbf{V}`$. Eligibility requires
a valid, completed evaluation with a gain over $`p_{t}`$ greater than
the margin $`\delta_{\mathrm{prom}}`$; $`p_{t}`$ continues when none
qualifies. Thus $`p_{t+1}=(\mathbf{H}_{t+1},\theta_{t+1})`$ preserves
the strongest validated outcome of inheritance and adaptation. All
completed outcomes, including unsuccessful modifications, enter
$`\mathbf{A}_{<t+1}`$ with harness ancestry and model provenance
(checkpoint coefficients $`\boldsymbol{\alpha}`$ and training history)
to inform later inheritance.

## 4  Experiment

### 4.1  Experimental Setup

#### Evaluation benchmarks.

To test whether co-evolution generalizes beyond a single harness design,
we evaluate CoEvo-RSI on three domains that demand different harness
capabilities: long-trajectory reasoning, policy-constrained tool use,
and structured device control. ❶ Failure attribution identifies the
responsible agent (Who) and the decisive error step (When) in
multi-agent trajectories. We hold out 200 TracerTraj ([Zhang et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib69)) instances for validation during evolution, leaving
3,400 single-error training instances drawn from the remaining
TracerTraj data, CORRECT-Error ([Yu et al., 2026a](#bib.bib63)),
AFTraj ([Zhang et al., 2026a](#bib.bib67)), and self-constructed
trajectories. The Hand and Algo. subsets of Who&When ([Zhang et al.,
2025d](#bib.bib77)), Who&When Pro ([Liu et al., 2026a](#bib.bib23)), and
TraceElephant ([Chen et al., 2026a](#bib.bib7)) are reserved for
out-of-distribution (OOD) testing. ❷ Role-aware text-to-SQL requires
generating SQL only when the user’s role authorizes every referenced
table and column, and refusing otherwise. We use the Spider subset of
the RBAC benchmark ([Fei et al., 2026](#bib.bib11)) with its official
split and its BIRD subset as an OOD test without any training.
❸ Smart-home instruction following maps instructions to device
operations and rejects infeasible ones. We use the valid (VM) and
invalid (IM) multi-device subsets of HomeBench ([Li et al.,
2025](#bib.bib21)) with official splits.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

#### Baselines.

We compare against four families. ◼ Direct LLMs: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash,
DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813, GLM-5.3, MiniMax-M3, and Qwen3.8-Max, all with
high thinking effort. ◼ Harness-enhanced systems: for failure
attribution, CHIEF ([Wang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib53)) and FALAT ([Rafi
et al., 2026](#bib.bib41)) with MiniMax-2.5, AgentScope ([Bi et al.,
2026](#bib.bib6)) with GPT-5.1, and DCFA ([Wang et al.,
2026c](#bib.bib54)) with GPT-5, with results taken from their papers;
for text-to-SQL, OpenCode ([Anomaly, 2025](#bib.bib2)),
mini-SWE-agent ([Yang et al., 2024](#bib.bib59)), and Pi ([Zechner,
2025](#bib.bib66)) paired with frontier LLMs. ◼ Harness evolution:
Meta-Harness ([Lee et al., 2026c](#bib.bib20)) and Self-Harness ([Zhang
et al., 2026d](#bib.bib72)), sharing the task model, meta-agent LLM, and
number of rounds with CoEvo-RSI. ◼ Model training: GRPO ([Shao et al.,
2024](#bib.bib42)) and GSPO ([Zheng et al., 2025](#bib.bib83)) applied
under the initial harness. ◼ Model-harness Co-Evolution:
HarnessForge ([Chen et al., 2026b](#bib.bib8)).

#### Implementation.

We evolve Qwen3.5-9B ([Qwen Team, 2026](#bib.bib40)) from a hand-written
initial harness, using DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (high reasoning effort) in
Codex ([OpenAI, 2025](#bib.bib35)) as the meta-agent. Each run has ten
rounds with $`\mathbf{K}{=}8`$ harness candidates per round. The
selected Qwen3.5-9B checkpoint samples up to three trajectories per
training task under its paired harness at temperature 1, stopping at the
first verifier-accepted one. The accepted trajectories are used for one
epoch of full-parameter SFT (learning rate 5e-6, batch size 8) on four
H100 GPUs. Full data, hyperparameter, baseline, and prompt details are
in
[Appendices A](#A1 "Appendix A Experimental Details ‣ When Harnesses Evolve, Which Models Should Follow?")
and [E](#A5 "Appendix E Meta-Agent Prompts ‣ When Harnesses Evolve, Which Models Should Follow?").

### 4.2  Main Results

#### Failure attribution.

We first examine whether co-evolving a small model with its harness can
outperform much larger models and single-sided evolution.
[Table 1](#S4.T1 "In Baselines. ‣ 4.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4 Experiment ‣ When Harnesses Evolve, Which Models Should Follow?")
compares the co-evolved 9B agent with all four baseline families. On
Who&When Hand, CoEvo-RSI reaches 68.39% Who and 29.31% When accuracy,
ahead of the strongest harness-enhanced system FALAT + MiniMax-2.5
(66.30% and 25.90%). On Who&When Algo., it obtains 62.17% Who and 44.71%
When accuracy, compared with the strongest baseline scores of 68.25% and
47.62%, respectively. On the other OOD benchmarks, CoEvo-RSI attains
69.43% Who accuracy on Who&When Pro, above Qwen3.8-Max (65.03%), and
70.78% on TraceElephant, 14.16 points above DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813
(56.62%). Single-sided evolution falls short: Self-Harness trails
CoEvo-RSI by 11.49 Who points on Who&When Hand, and on TraceElephant
both harness evolution baselines drop below 10% When accuracy while
CoEvo-RSI retains 28.92%; the RL baselines trained under the initial
harness likewise trail CoEvo-RSI in Who accuracy on every benchmark,
although they attain higher When accuracy on Who&When Pro and
TraceElephant.
[Figure 4](#S4.F4 "In Failure attribution. ‣ 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiment ‣ When Harnesses Evolve, Which Models Should Follow?")
shows how these gains accumulate: over ten rounds, AA improves by 11.11
points and SA by 5.55 points while TIMR stays at or below 0.22%. The
strongest gains appear on Who&When Hand and in agent attribution on
Who&When Pro and TraceElephant, showing the task-dependent benefits of
model–harness alignment.

The left panel compares full CoEvo-RSI with Harness-only, Model-only,

#### Role-aware text-to-SQL.

We next examine access control and query execution under co-evolution.
[Table 2](#S4.T2 "In Failure attribution. ‣ 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiment ‣ When Harnesses Evolve, Which Models Should Follow?")
compares CoEvo-RSI with direct LLMs and general-purpose coding
harnesses. On Spider, CoEvo-RSI achieves the best Safe-EX (80.85%),
Safe-Deny (96.64%), and violation rate (1.57%), surpassing Pi +
MiniMax-M3 (80.26%, 96.33%, and 1.72%).
[Figure 5](#S4.F5 "In Role-aware text-to-SQL. ‣ 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiment ‣ When Harnesses Evolve, Which Models Should Follow?")
traces these gains: the harness successively acquires evidence checking,
reference-level authorization, and verification with repair, raising
Safe-EX from 77.09% to 80.85% and cutting the violation rate from 2.00%
to 1.57%, a 21.5% relative reduction. On the OOD BIRD subset, its
Safe-EX is close to GLM-5.3 (60.15% vs. 60.90%), alongside the highest
Safe-Deny (91.26%), the lowest violation rate (5.65%), and the
second-best AC-F1 (90.24%). These results indicate promising
cross-database transfer for a 9B model. The safety–utility balance may
partly reflect more conservative refusal, which can improve policy
compliance while limiting successful execution of authorized queries.

Blue circles and purple squares track Safe-EX and violation rate on the

#### Smart-home instruction following.

Finally, we examine whether co-evolution transfers to structured device
control.
[Table 3](#S4.T3 "In Smart-home instruction following. ‣ 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiment ‣ When Harnesses Evolve, Which Models Should Follow?")
compares CoEvo-RSI with direct LLMs on two multi-device subsets. On
valid instructions (VM), CoEvo-RSI achieves the best success rate
(75.51%) and F1 (89.23%), ahead of DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813 (75.10% and
89.18%). On invalid instructions (IM), it ties for the best success rate
(84.54%) and obtains the highest F1 (91.80%). Thus, the co-evolved agent
both executes feasible operations and rejects infeasible ones at the
level of much larger models.

### 4.3  Ablation Study

We compare full CoEvo-RSI with three variants over ten rounds on
Who&When Algo.
([Figure 4](#S4.F4 "In Failure attribution. ‣ 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiment ‣ When Harnesses Evolve, Which Models Should Follow?")):
Harness-only evolves the harness with a frozen model; Model-only trains
under the initial harness; and Latest-only co-evolves both using only
the latest generation. ❶ Joint evolution. Harness-only has lower SA than
full CoEvo-RSI in every round and TIMR above 1% in eight of ten rounds,
versus at most 0.22% for full CoEvo-RSI. Model-only maintains near-zero
TIMR with SA at most 35%, indicating that interface compatibility alone
is insufficient for task success. ❷ Historical reuse. Latest-only
regresses at round 4 and finishes with the lowest SA. Full CoEvo-RSI
recovers from its round-4 dip, reusing round-4 weights with new
harnesses at rounds 6 and 8 to reach 61.11% and 61.90% AA. Together,
these results support complementary roles for bidirectional inheritance
and historical reuse in task performance, interface compatibility, and
recovery.

### 4.4  Framework Analysis

#### Robustness and Stability Analysis.

We assess sensitivity to the search budget by varying the number of
harness candidates per round $`\mathbf{K}\in\{4,6,8,10\}`$ with all
other settings fixed
([Figure 6](#S4.F6 "In Robustness and Stability Analysis. ‣ 4.4 Framework Analysis ‣ 4 Experiment ‣ When Harnesses Evolve, Which Models Should Follow?")(a–c)).
AA stays between 45.11% and 52.17%, SA between 28.80% and 37.50%, and
TIMR at or below 0.12% for every $`\mathbf{K}`$. These results support
the robustness of CoEvo-RSI across the tested candidate budgets. We also
examine inference cost–accuracy trade-offs in
[Figure 7](#S4.F7 "In Robustness and Stability Analysis. ‣ 4.4 Framework Analysis ‣ 4 Experiment ‣ When Harnesses Evolve, Which Models Should Follow?").

Figure 6: Sensitivity to the number of harness candidates $`\mathbf{K}`$
(three rounds, single run): (a) AA, (b) SA, (c) TIMR, (d) run span, (e)
evaluation time, (f) API cost. Each bar corresponds to
$`\mathbf{K}\in\{4,6,8,10\}`$, with the remaining settings fixed. The
top row reports held-out task performance and interface violations,
while the bottom row summarizes wall-clock run span, evaluation time,
and API expenditure. The tested budgets maintain low TIMR with modest
variation in accuracy; the default $`\mathbf{K}{=}8`$ gives the shortest
run span of 17.48 hours at an API cost of \$2.72.

Figure 7: Inference cost–accuracy trade-offs. CoEvo-RSI uses
OpenRouter’s Qwen3.5-9B pricing. The left and right panels report Who

a full evaluation pass, using a logarithmic cost axis. Dashed staircases
and shaded regions summarize the baseline Pareto frontiers, while stars
mark the co-evolved 9B agent.

![Refer to caption](2610.25078v1/lineage-heatmap-coevox.png)

Figure 8: Interface compatibility on RBAC. Normalized TIMR
($`\downarrow`$) across harness–checkpoint pairs; only the lower
triangle is available during evolution. Rows index evolved harnesses and
columns index model checkpoints, with TIMR globally min–max scaled to

#### Cost Analysis.

We analyze training cost and inference cost separately. ❶ Training cost.
Across the three-round co-evolution runs in
[Figure 6](#S4.F6 "In Robustness and Stability Analysis. ‣ 4.4 Framework Analysis ‣ 4 Experiment ‣ When Harnesses Evolve, Which Models Should Follow?")(d–f),
API expenditure ranges from \$2.06 to \$3.69. All runs finish within a
day (17.48–20.71 hours), with evaluation taking 4.54–6.11 hours. Our
default $`\mathbf{K}{=}8`$ achieves the shortest run span of 17.48 hours
at an API cost of \$2.72. We also compare training rollout budgets
([Table 8](#A1.T8 "In Training-sample budget. ‣ A.5 Baseline Configurations ‣ Appendix A Experimental Details ‣ When Harnesses Evolve, Which Models Should Follow?")):
across ten rounds, CoEvo-RSI costs fewer rollout budgets than GRPO/GSPO
and achieves higher agent accuracy on all four failure-attribution
benchmarks
([Table 1](#S4.T1 "In Baselines. ‣ 4.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4 Experiment ‣ When Harnesses Evolve, Which Models Should Follow?")).
❷ Inference cost.
[Figure 7](#S4.F7 "In Robustness and Stability Analysis. ‣ 4.4 Framework Analysis ‣ 4 Experiment ‣ When Harnesses Evolve, Which Models Should Follow?")
plots Who accuracy on Who&When Hand and Safe-EX on RBAC Spider against
the API cost of a full evaluation pass, which for Who&When covers both
the Hand and Algo. subsets. On Who&When Hand, CoEvo-RSI reaches 68.39%
at \$0.16, compared with 60.34% at \$3.55 for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, a
gain of 8.05 points at $`22\times`$ lower cost. On RBAC Spider, it
exceeds the strongest baseline, Pi + MiniMax-M3, by 0.59 Safe-EX points
at $`38\times`$ lower cost.

#### Inheritance Analysis.

[Figure 8](#S4.F8 "In Robustness and Stability Analysis. ‣ 4.4 Framework Analysis ‣ 4 Experiment ‣ When Harnesses Evolve, Which Models Should Follow?")
pairs every selected harness with every checkpoint from the RBAC run.
Only the lower triangle reflects real choices, since round $`i`$ can
pair $`\mathbf{H}_{i}`$ only with checkpoints up to $`\mathrm{M}_{i}`$.
❶ A growing archive improves interface compatibility. As candidates grow
from one to ten checkpoints, the selected pairs move toward low TIMR in
the bottom-right corner (mean normalized TIMR from about 0.72 in rounds
1–3 to 0.13 in rounds 6–10), and in seven of ten rounds the selected
checkpoint is the lowest-TIMR one available. ❷ Inheritance reaches back
into the archive. Five rounds re-select existing weights, and every
later derived checkpoint merges with the round-3 checkpoint. Round 10
reuses that checkpoint: with high TIMR under harnesses 4–9 (0.54–1.00),
it has the lowest TIMR under the final harness (0.02) and attains the
best Safe-EX of the run (80.85%). Interface compatibility is
pair-specific; latest-only inheritance misses such pairs.

## 5  Conclusion

We presented CoEvo-RSI, a bi-level framework that addresses the
brain–body mismatch problem in model–harness co-evolution through
agent-driven, bidirectional historical inheritance. A shared
evolutionary archive and execution feedback guide harness development
from historical designs, model checkpoint selection or merging, and
subsequent adaptation under the selected harness. Using only SFT on its
own rejection-sampled trajectories, CoEvo-RSI makes a compact task model
competitive with larger models across multi-agent failure attribution,
role-aware text-to-SQL, and smart-home instruction following. Together,
these findings highlight brain–body alignment as a central consideration
for self-improving agents and bidirectional historical inheritance as a
practical route to evolving execution scaffolds (body) and intrinsic
capabilities (brain) together.

## Appendix A Experimental Details

This section details the benchmarks, data, initial harnesses, and
hyperparameters behind
[Section 4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4 Experiment ‣ When Harnesses Evolve, Which Models Should Follow?").
In every domain, training, validation, and test sets are disjoint at the
level of sample IDs, tasks, and trajectories. The same validation set
$`\mathbf{V}`$ guides harness and checkpoint selection and promotion
during evolution; test sets are reserved for performance reporting. For
failure attribution, all 200 validation instances are held out from
TracerTraj and removed from the training pool
([Section A.2](#A1.SS2 "A.2 Failure Attribution ‣ Appendix A Experimental Details ‣ When Harnesses Evolve, Which Models Should Follow?")).

### A.1  Common Setup

#### Evolution.

All domains run ten rounds of co-evolution with $`\mathbf{K}{=}8`$
harness candidates per round. The candidate-sensitivity study in
[Section 4.4](#S4.SS4 "4.4 Framework Analysis ‣ 4 Experiment ‣ When Harnesses Evolve, Which Models Should Follow?")
is the exception and uses three rounds. The meta-agent is
DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash with high reasoning effort, running inside Codex. In
each round, the meta-agent receives validation rollouts of the incumbent
model–harness pair. Each editor browses the historical archive, selects
an inheritance base, and develops a copy of that harness using the
execution evidence and reusable historical designs. The prompt it
receives is listed in
[Appendix E](#A5 "Appendix E Meta-Agent Prompts ‣ When Harnesses Evolve, Which Models Should Follow?").
Each candidate is then evaluated on the full validation set. Candidates
are compared using the domain-specific objectives in
[Table 4](#A1.T4 "In Model training. ‣ A.1 Common Setup ‣ Appendix A Experimental Details ‣ When Harnesses Evolve, Which Models Should Follow?").

#### Task model and rollout.

The task model is Qwen3.5-9B ([Qwen Team, 2026](#bib.bib40)) with
thinking enabled at high reasoning effort. It is served with vLLM and
sampled with temperature $`1.0`$, top-$`p`$ $`0.95`$, and top-$`k`$
$`20`$. Per-domain generation budgets, context lengths, and turn limits
appear in
[Table 4](#A1.T4 "In Model training. ‣ A.1 Common Setup ‣ Appendix A Experimental Details ‣ When Harnesses Evolve, Which Models Should Follow?").

#### Model training.

For each training task, the selected model $`\bar{\theta}_{t}`$ samples
up to three trajectories under its paired harness
$`\bar{\mathbf{H}}_{t}`$, stopping at the first verifier-accepted one.
These accepted trajectories, together with selected high-quality
accepted trajectories replayed from earlier rounds, are used for one
epoch of full-parameter SFT of the same model with ms-swift ([Zhao
et al., 2024](#bib.bib81)). Training uses AdamW with learning rate
$`5\times 10^{-6}`$, a cosine schedule with 3% warmup, a per-device
batch size of 1, and 4 gradient-accumulation steps. It runs on four H100
GPUs with DeepSpeed ZeRO-3, bf16, and gradient checkpointing. The global
batch size is 8 in all domains, and long-context domains additionally
use sequence parallelism of size 2.

|                     |                |                  |               |
|---------------------|----------------|------------------|---------------|
|                     |  Attribution   |  RBAC            |  HomeBench    |
| Rollout             |                |                  |               |
|  Max new tokens     |  8,192         |  4,096           |  8,192        |
|  Context length     |  65,536        |  32,768          |  65,536       |
|  Max agent turns    |  20            |  10              |  20           |
| SFT                 |                |                  |               |
|  Max seq. length    |  65,536        |  8,192           |  65,536       |
|  Sequence parallel  |  2             |  1               |  2            |
|  Global batch size  |  8             |  8               |  8            |
| Selection           |                |                  |               |
|  Metrics            |  AA, SA (3:7)  |  Safe-EX, AC-F1  |  Success, F1  |

Table 4: Per-domain settings. Selection metrics are computed on the
validation set following the objectives in the meta-agent prompts
([Appendix E](#A5 "Appendix E Meta-Agent Prompts ‣ When Harnesses Evolve, Which Models Should Follow?")).
AA and SA denote agent and step accuracy.

### A.2  Failure Attribution

#### Task.

Given the full log of a failed multi-agent run, the system must name the
agent responsible for the failure (Who) and the decisive step at which
the failure becomes unrecoverable (When).

#### Benchmarks.

[Table 5](#A1.T5 "In Benchmarks. ‣ A.2 Failure Attribution ‣ Appendix A Experimental Details ‣ When Harnesses Evolve, Which Models Should Follow?")
lists all splits; all four test benchmarks are held out from training
and evolutionary selection. Who&When ([Zhang et al., 2025d](#bib.bib77))
contains 58 hand-crafted (Hand) and 126 algorithm-generated (Algo.)
trajectories. Who&When Pro ([Liu et al., 2026a](#bib.bib23)) is
evaluated on its 1,750 multi-agent, text-only trajectories; we exclude
single-agent trajectories, on which attribution is nearly saturated. For
TraceElephant ([Chen et al., 2026a](#bib.bib7)), we drop records whose
decisive-step annotation is missing or invalid, which leaves 219
evaluable instances.

|            |                                        |         |
|------------|----------------------------------------|---------|
| Split      | Composition                            | \#Inst. |
| Train      | TracerTraj 1,618; CORRECT-Error 1,230; | 3,400   |
|            | AFTraj 430; self-constructed 122       |         |
| Validation | TracerTraj (held out)                  | 200     |
| Test (OOD) | Who&When Hand                          | 58      |
| Test (OOD) | Who&When Algo.                         | 126     |
| Test (OOD) | Who&When Pro (multi-agent, text-only)  | 1,750   |
| Test (OOD) | TraceElephant (evaluable)              | 219     |

Table 5: Failure attribution data. The 200 validation instances are held
out from TracerTraj and excluded from training, and all four test
benchmarks are reserved for OOD evaluation.

#### Training and validation data.

Training instances come from TracerTraj ([Zhang et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib69)), CORRECT-Error ([Yu et al., 2026a](#bib.bib63)),
AFTraj ([Zhang et al., 2026a](#bib.bib67)), and a small set of
trajectories we construct ourselves. We keep only trajectories that
contain a single error, use dense one-based step indices, and have a
responsible agent consistent with the decisive step. Of the 1,818
filtered TracerTraj instances, 200 are held out for validation and the
remaining 1,618 are retained for training. Together with 1,230
CORRECT-Error, 430 AFTraj, and 122 self-constructed instances, this
gives 3,400 training instances. The 200-instance TracerTraj validation
set guides candidate and checkpoint selection and promotion. The source
studies explicitly document evaluation-data isolation in their
respective protocols ([Zhang et al., 2025b](#bib.bib69); [Yu et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib63); [Zhang et al., 2026a](#bib.bib67)). We further
rigorously checked our training data against the held-out TracerTraj
validation set, Who&When Hand, Who&When Algo., Who&When Pro, and
TraceElephant. These checks confirmed separation at the sample-ID and
task levels and found no identical or highly similar trajectories across
training and evaluation.

#### Metrics.

Agent accuracy (AA, reported as Who) is the fraction of instances whose
predicted responsible agent matches the annotation. Step accuracy (SA,
reported as When) is the fraction whose predicted decisive step matches
the annotated step exactly. The harness requires the model to answer
through a structured final_answer tool, so predictions are parsed and
scored by exact match against the ground truth without an LLM judge.
Results are reported separately for each subset.

#### Initial harness.

The hand-written harness exposes the trajectory summary-first: the model
initially sees only per-step metadata such as step IDs and agent names.
It must call inspect to read the full content of a step, and it submits
the agent and step through final_answer. Ground-truth labels are never
exposed, and the episode is limited to 20 turns.

### A.3  Role-Aware Text-to-SQL

#### Task.

Each instance pairs a natural-language question over a database with a
user role whose column- and operation-level access policy is given. A
request is authorized only if every table, column, and operation it
needs is covered by the role’s policy ([Fei et al., 2026](#bib.bib11)).
For authorized requests, the system must return SQL that executes to the
reference result. Otherwise, it must refuse.

#### Benchmarks and data.

[Table 6](#A1.T6 "In Benchmarks and data. ‣ A.3 Role-Aware Text-to-SQL ‣ Appendix A Experimental Details ‣ When Harnesses Evolve, Which Models Should Follow?")
lists all splits. Training and evolution use only the Spider subset. The
8,000 training instances and 2,000 validation instances are disjoint
samples from the official training split. Test results are reported on
the full Spider test set and on the full BIRD subset, which is never
used for training or evolution and therefore measures pure
generalization to unseen databases.

|            |                          |         |      |
|------------|--------------------------|---------|------|
| Split      | Source                   | \#Inst. | \#DB |
| Train      | Spider (train)           | 8,000   | –    |
| Validation | Spider (train, held out) | 2,000   | –    |
| Test (ID)  | Spider (test)            | 6,926   | 20   |
| Test (OOD) | BIRD                     | 10,175  | 11   |

Table 6: Role-aware text-to-SQL data. Instances are role–query pairs,
and BIRD is used only for testing.

#### Metrics.

Following [Fei et al. (2026)](#bib.bib11), each prediction falls into
one of six outcomes, determined by the ground-truth decision and the
system’s response:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | Answered with SQL |  |  |
| Ground truth | exec. correct | exec. wrong | Refused |
| Allow ($`\mathbf{N}_{+}`$) | $`\mathbf{S}_{\mathrm{c}}`$ | $`\mathbf{S}_{\mathrm{w}}`$ | $`\mathbf{S}_{\mathrm{or}}`$ |
| Deny ($`\mathbf{N}_{-}`$) | $`\mathbf{S}_{\mathrm{vc}}`$ | $`\mathbf{S}_{\mathrm{vw}}`$ | $`\mathbf{S}_{\mathrm{pr}}`$ |

The sets $`\mathbf{S}_{\mathrm{c}}`$, $`\mathbf{S}_{\mathrm{w}}`$,
$`\mathbf{S}_{\mathrm{or}}`$, $`\mathbf{S}_{\mathrm{vc}}`$,
$`\mathbf{S}_{\mathrm{vw}}`$, and $`\mathbf{S}_{\mathrm{pr}}`$ contain
correct, wrong, over-refused, violation-correct, violation-wrong, and
properly refused predictions, respectively. An allowed request answered
with policy-violating SQL also belongs to $`\mathbf{S}_{\mathrm{vc}}`$
or $`\mathbf{S}_{\mathrm{vw}}`$. SQL correctness is judged by execution
equivalence on the sample database. Let $`\mathbf{N}_{+}`$ and
$`\mathbf{N}_{-}`$ count allowed and denied requests, with total
$`\mathbf{N}=\mathbf{N}_{+}+\mathbf{N}_{-}`$. Define
$`n_{\mathrm{ans}}=|\mathbf{S}_{\mathrm{c}}|+|\mathbf{S}_{\mathrm{w}}|`$,
$`n_{\mathrm{viol}}=|\mathbf{S}_{\mathrm{vc}}|+|\mathbf{S}_{\mathrm{vw}}|`$,
and $`n_{\mathrm{ref}}=|\mathbf{S}_{\mathrm{or}}|`$. The metrics are

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\begin{gathered}\text{Safe-EX}=\frac{|\mathbf{S}_{\mathrm{c}}|}{\mathbf{N}_{+}},\qquad\text{Safe-Deny}=\frac{|\mathbf{S}_{\mathrm{pr}}|}{\mathbf{N}_{-}},\\[5.0pt]
\text{Viol.}=\frac{n_{\mathrm{viol}}}{\mathbf{N}},\qquad\text{Over-ref.}=\frac{n_{\mathrm{ref}}}{\mathbf{N}},\\[5.0pt]
\text{AC-F1}=\frac{2n_{\mathrm{ans}}}{2n_{\mathrm{ans}}+n_{\mathrm{viol}}+n_{\mathrm{ref}}}.\end{gathered}
``` |  |

For selection, we additionally track the LLM rate, which is the fraction
of instances that reach the LLM, together with the coverage and accuracy
of rule-based decisions.

#### Initial harness.

The hand-written harness first applies deterministic rule routing, which
links the question to schema columns and checks them against the role
policy. When the rules are not confident, it falls back to a multi-turn
LLM agent with two tools: test_sql executes a query on the database and
returns rows or an error, and final_answer submits the access decision
together with SQL when access is granted. The agent is limited to 10
turns.

### A.4  Smart-Home Instruction Following

#### Task.

Each HomeBench ([Li et al., 2025](#bib.bib21)) query bundles 2 to 10
sub-instructions for devices in a simulated home. The system must emit
one device command per feasible sub-instruction and an error for each
infeasible one, such as a missing device or an unsupported operation. We
use the VM and IM subsets, which contain only valid and only invalid
multi-device queries, respectively.

#### Data.

[Table 7](#A1.T7 "In Data. ‣ A.4 Smart-Home Instruction Following ‣ Appendix A Experimental Details ‣ When Harnesses Evolve, Which Models Should Follow?")
lists the splits. The 10,000 training instances are sampled from the
official training split, and 2,000 further training-split instances are
held out as the validation set. The official multi-device test set is
used only for the final report.

|            |         |
|------------|---------|
| Split      | \#Inst. |
| Train      | 10,000  |
| Validation | 2,000   |
| Test       | 342     |

Table 7: HomeBench data. Validation is held out from the official
training split.

#### Metrics.

Success is the exact match between the predicted and reference command
multisets, including error outputs. F1 is the micro-averaged
command-level F1 under the same official counting. Both are computed
with the official scorer.

#### Initial harness.

The hand-written harness gives the model a compact index of rooms and
devices together with four official in-context examples, and the
meta-agent may also edit these examples. Detailed device states and
method signatures are available only through the read-only tools
inspect_home and list_methods, and the model submits its commands
through final_answer. The episode is limited to 20 turns.

### A.5  Baseline Configurations

#### Harness evolution.

We run Meta-Harness ([Lee et al., 2026c](#bib.bib20)) and
Self-Harness ([Zhang et al., 2026d](#bib.bib72)) from their official
implementations and add a failure attribution domain adapter for each.
Both start from the same task model (Qwen3.5-9B), the same hand-written
initial harness, and the same 200 held-out TracerTraj validation
instances as CoEvo-RSI. Each runs for ten rounds. The task-model weights
remain frozen throughout harness evolution. Both baselines use the same
meta-agent LLM and settings as CoEvo-RSI, namely DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash
with high reasoning effort, and each keeps its officially recommended
proposer workflow. Meta-Harness drives the LLM through Codex and
proposes eight candidates per round. Self-Harness uses its native
multi-proposer workflow, which calls the LLM directly without a coding
agent, and explores eight candidates per round. Each candidate in both
baselines is evaluated twice on the validation set.

#### Model training.

GRPO ([Shao et al., 2024](#bib.bib42)) and GSPO ([Zheng et al.,
2025](#bib.bib83)) train Qwen3.5-9B under the initial harness on the
same 3,400 training instances with verl ([Sheng et al.,
2024](#bib.bib44)). The two runs share all settings except the policy
loss
([Table 9](#A1.T9 "In Training-sample budget. ‣ A.5 Baseline Configurations ‣ Appendix A Experimental Details ‣ When Harnesses Evolve, Which Models Should Follow?")).
Both use group-normalized advantages and no KL penalty.

#### Training-sample budget.

[Table 8](#A1.T8 "In Training-sample budget. ‣ A.5 Baseline Configurations ‣ Appendix A Experimental Details ‣ When Harnesses Evolve, Which Models Should Follow?")
compares the trajectories each method samples and trains on. A single RL
run samples 3,400 prompts $`\times`$ 8 rollouts $`\times`$ 3 epochs and
updates on every rollout. Across all ten rounds, CoEvo-RSI samples 8.5%
fewer trajectories than one RL run and fine-tunes on 39,395
verifier-accepted trajectories, including replayed ones, which is 48.3%
of the RL training samples, while also evolving the harness.

| Method                | Sampled | Trained on |
|-----------------------|---------|------------|
| GRPO / GSPO (each)    | 81,600  | 81,600     |
| CoEvo-RSI (10 rounds) | 74,639  | 39,395     |

## Appendix B Scope and Interpretation of TIMR

#### Diagnostic scope.

TIMR
([Equation 5](#S3.E5 "In Diagnosing interface mismatch. ‣ 3.1 Model–Harness Co-Evolution ‣ 3 Method ‣ When Harnesses Evolve, Which Models Should Follow?"))
measures the frequency of observable interface violations within a
model–harness pair: calls to unavailable tools, interface-contract
violations, and malformed outputs. These events expose a concrete aspect
of brain–body mismatch at the execution boundary and can be checked
directly from traces. Their low verification cost makes TIMR useful for
diagnosing candidate pairs during evolution. The broader problem
definition also covers learned capabilities that a harness underuses or
constrains. Such cases can produce valid tool calls throughout an
unsuccessful trajectory; assessing them requires task outcomes and
examination of the information and actions the harness makes available.
TIMR therefore provides a focused operational view of interface
compatibility within this broader evaluation. Raw TIMR lies in $`[0,1]`$
($`0`$–$`100\%`$);
[Figure 8](#S4.F8 "In Robustness and Stability Analysis. ‣ 4.4 Framework Analysis ‣ 4 Experiment ‣ When Harnesses Evolve, Which Models Should Follow?")
uses global min–max scaling across all harness–checkpoint pairs to
$`[0,1]`$.

#### Relationship to task performance.

Task success depends jointly on interface use, reasoning, access to
relevant evidence, and the execution workflow. The ablations in
[Figure 4](#S4.F4 "In Failure attribution. ‣ 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiment ‣ When Harnesses Evolve, Which Models Should Follow?")
illustrate these distinct factors: Model-only maintains near-zero TIMR
with step accuracy at most 35%, whereas Harness-only has TIMR above 1%
in eight of ten rounds and lower step accuracy than full CoEvo-RSI in
every round. Full CoEvo-RSI keeps TIMR at or below 0.22% while improving
task performance. These observations support using TIMR together with
task scores to distinguish execution friction from other performance
bottlenecks. They provide diagnostic evidence; attributing a performance
gain specifically to lower TIMR would require controlled interventions
that isolate interface behavior from changes in reasoning, information
access, and execution budget.

#### Role in co-evolution.

CoEvo-RSI reads TIMR alongside task performance when proposing
checkpoint selections or merges, and uses validation task scores to
select and promote model–harness pairs
([Equations 12](#S3.E12 "In Model inheritance and selection. ‣ 3.3 Model Inheritance ‣ 3 Method ‣ When Harnesses Evolve, Which Models Should Follow?")
and [13](#S3.E13 "Equation 13 ‣ Pair-specific adaptation and promotion. ‣ 3.3 Model Inheritance ‣ 3 Method ‣ When Harnesses Evolve, Which Models Should Follow?")).
A low TIMR identifies a pair whose observed interactions largely satisfy
the harness’s interface requirements; task evaluation establishes how
effectively that pair solves the intended problems. This division gives
TIMR a practical role as an inexpensive diagnostic signal, with the
value of an evolutionary update assessed through downstream performance.

## Appendix C Interpreting Comparisons with Frontier Models

Our evaluation asks how far co-evolution can bring a compact task model
toward frontier-level performance in a given domain. The compared models
start from markedly different capability levels: on the Artificial
Analysis Intelligence Index v4.3.2, Qwen3.5-9B (Reasoning) scores 11,
compared with 36 for DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813 (Max) and 45 for GLM-5.3
(Max) ([Artificial Analysis, 2026a](#bib.bib3); [Artificial Analysis,
2026b](#bib.bib4); [Artificial Analysis, 2026c](#bib.bib5)). These
independent measurements contextualize the capability gap behind our
task comparisons. Against this background, approaching or matching
frontier systems on several demanding tasks is a substantive outcome for
a 9B model. For example, CoEvo-RSI achieves 95.51% Spider AC-F1 against
95.85% for the strongest system on this metric, Pi + MiniMax-M3
([Table 2](#S4.T2 "In Failure attribution. ‣ 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiment ‣ When Harnesses Evolve, Which Models Should Follow?")),
and 75.51% HomeBench VM success against 75.10% for DeepSeek-V4-Pro
([Table 3](#S4.T3 "In Smart-home instruction following. ‣ 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiment ‣ When Harnesses Evolve, Which Models Should Follow?")).
Such proximity remains meaningful when individual metric rankings vary
across benchmarks.

All SFT supervision comes from Qwen3.5-9B’s own verifier-accepted
trajectories, generated by the selected checkpoint or, through replay,
by earlier checkpoints and retained through rejection sampling
([Section A.1](#A1.SS1 "A.1 Common Setup ‣ Appendix A Experimental Details ‣ When Harnesses Evolve, Which Models Should Follow?")).
The meta-agent guides harness evolution and checkpoint inheritance;
model training consolidates the 9B task model’s successful execution
experience. We view the resulting competitiveness as evidence of how
much useful capability can be elicited and consolidated from a compact
model through coordinated model–harness evolution.

#### Positioning: affordable domain specialization.

As frontier models advance, a complementary deployment need is to make
compact models effective within a well-defined domain. We position
CoEvo-RSI as a tool for this need, particularly for frequent agent calls
where cost and response-time budgets shape system design. Potential
applications include device manufacturers integrating smart-home control
and RL systems requiring failure-attribution feedback on repeated agent
rollouts. These needs motivate our three benchmark domains: smart-home
instruction following for device execution, multi-agent failure
attribution for automated diagnosis, and role-aware text-to-SQL for
policy-constrained data access. Each tests task-specific behavior under
concrete operational requirements. The results support this practical
motivation: CoEvo-RSI achieves 68.39% agent accuracy on Who&When Hand
versus 60.34% for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash. Under the API pricing in
[Figure 7](#S4.F7 "In Robustness and Stability Analysis. ‣ 4.4 Framework Analysis ‣ 4 Experiment ‣ When Harnesses Evolve, Which Models Should Follow?"),
their full evaluation passes over Hand and Algo. cost \$0.16 and \$3.55,
respectively, approximately $`22\times`$ lower for CoEvo-RSI. Together
with the close Spider and HomeBench results above, this demonstrates the
value of specialization for delivering competitive task performance at
low recurring cost. Small differences on individual metrics can be
acceptable when the resulting agent meets an application’s quality
requirements and operating budget. Our aim is to give practitioners an
affordable model–harness pair optimized for the tasks they repeatedly
need to solve.

## Appendix D Comparison with Related Evolution Frameworks

[TABLE]

Table 10: Comparison of published evolution procedures. Select denotes
choosing model initialization from historical checkpoints independently
of the harness’s parent lineage; Merge denotes combining multiple
historical model checkpoints. Model updates list the main training
instantiations; “–” indicates a fixed model.

[Table 10](#A4.T10 "In Appendix D Comparison with Related Evolution Frameworks ‣ When Harnesses Evolve, Which Models Should Follow?")
compares six model–harness co-evolution methods and two harness-only
methods through the sources of their inherited structure and
capabilities. Harness history supports several forms of reuse, including
archive-guided refinement, search over previous programs, and persistent
component updates. On the model side, the compared co-evolution
procedures continue the current checkpoint or inherit the policy
associated with a parent branch. CoEvo-RSI makes both sources explicit
decisions over the evolutionary archive: harness editors choose
historical starting designs, and model inheritance independently selects
or merges historical checkpoints for the resulting harnesses. This
flexibility allows structure and capabilities from different generations
to form new candidate pairs, whose execution feedback guides selection
and subsequent adaptation. Bidirectional historical inheritance expands
the candidate space for further co-evolution.

## Appendix E Meta-Agent Prompts

The prompt given to the meta-agent in each round has two parts. The
first is a shared skeleton that is identical across domains (Prompt A)
and fixes the evidence discipline, workflow, and permission boundary.
The second is a domain direction (Prompts B–D) that is inserted at the
{domain direction} slot and states the domain’s metrics, interface
contract, and leakage constraints. Placeholders in braces are filled
with run-specific values. The prompts specify the shared evolution
workflow and domain-specific instructions, with file paths represented
by placeholders.
````
